chapter: Billy Pierce Studio and New York tap
title: The tap climate: Ruby Keeler, Cohan and Broadway revues
summary: Asked about the climate of tap in New York, Green speaks of Bradley's student Ruby Keeler, George M. Cohan, and Broadway's multi-talented shows.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Yes. Well, why don't you set the era? You know, in terms of the climate of dance. This was in what time period?
Well, I told you it was in 1930 -- what did I say? 1932, didn't I? February.
Uh-huh. And what was the climate then for tap dancing in New York? What was happening with tap dancing?

Well, the only thing that was happening with tap dancing then was Mr. Buddy Bradley's student, Ruby Keeler, she had tap dancing very popular, because she was a woman, see, and she was very clever. She could do those dances, you see. Buddy Bradley taught her things that excelled Bojangles, see. He made a champion out of her, you see. But she didn't have any competition, was the thing about it, see. Florence Mills had died, and you know.
What I mean really is what was the climate of New York then for performing tap dancers? Was tap dancing at its peak, were a lot of people doing it?
Oh, yeah. It had to be, because you understand --
George M. Cohan was a dancer. He was a dancer, and he was very famous. He had theatres. He had about four or five shows up and down Broadway, you know. He had had them, you
know. But at that time, then, see, I don't know, I mean. He didn't live too long. George M. Cohan didn't live too long after that, I think. He passed.

Wouldn't you say at that time that most people that were on Broadway, you had to be multi-talented? men and women The standard of the shows was so good, so high, usually they had to dance well, sing, be able to be -- it was really the great era of great revues, great shows. Ziegfeld.
